# Workshop 8
 
 # Building a Better Conversation: The Engaged California Model
 
 **Speakers:** [Jeffery Marino](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/jeffery-marino-25962610) (Director, Office of Data and Innovation, State of California), [Micah Weinberg](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/micah-weinberg-b5a819) (Nonresident Scholar, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace).
 
 This session presented [Engaged California](https:/engaged.ca.gov) , a state-sponsored digital deliberation program that used AI-powered analysis to turn thousands of resident comments into actionable policy recommendations following the Los Angeles wildfires. The project represents one of the most ambitious government-led experiments in participatory engagement in the United States, combining purpose-built platforms with intergovernmental coordination across state, county, and city levels.
 
 The speakers were Jeffery Marino, who leads the program at California's Office of Data and Innovation (ODI), and Micah Weinberg from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, who provided methodology guidance and framing. Their presentation focused less on the technology itself and more on what Weinberg called "the even cooler part" — the intergovernmental relations work required to make digital engagement produce real policy outcomes in a state as complex as California.
 
 ### 
 
 ### Origins and political will
 
 Governor Newsom's interest in deliberative democracy dates back over a decade, but Marino emphasized that this interest only materialized into a working program once ODI had built sufficient internal capacity in the form of data scientists, user experience designers, community engagement expertise, etc. "One reason it's so rare to see something like this sponsored by a government entity," Marino explained, "is that an elected official must commit to delivering outcomes before those needs have been communicated by the public—a big risk."
 
 The team had been preparing to launch with a pilot on social media's impact on youth when the LA fires struck in early 2025. The governor redirected the program immediately as wildfire recovery became the top statewide priority. Marino recalled significant internal resistance as advisors warned against piloting new technology during a crisis. "We heard from many people: 'Don't do it. Too risky. Too sensitive.'" But Newsom insisted the program proceed. That executive commitment, Weinberg noted, was essential: "This isn't a partisan point-scoring exercise; it's complex and hard. You wouldn't choose this as a political stunt."
 
 ### 
 
 ### The two-phase engagement structure
 
 The engagement ran in two distinct phases, each designed to avoid what Weinberg called "open-washing,” meaning the *appearance* of public input without genuine responsiveness.
 
 The first phase was agenda-setting. Rather than coming to residents with predetermined policy options, the team asked open-ended questions: "What is it that you want to be talking about? What are the things you want to deliberate on?" Program design partner [Avre Valentine of the Public Good Group](https:/publicgoodgroup.com/zabrae-valentine) advised asking the most open-ended question possible at this stage. The initial engagement included what Weinberg called a "throat-clearing" prompt — "Anything you want to tell us?" — before introducing any structure. This generated the raw material in the form of over 2,500 comments from more than 3,000 invited participants between March and August.
 
 The second phase brought synthesized findings back to participants, asking them to prioritize among options and specify which level of government should act. This is where the intergovernmental coordination became critical. The team had worked with LA County and LA City officials from the start to ensure that whatever recommendations emerged could actually be implemented. The report being released captures this second phase, including the 19 policy recommendations that emerged.
 
 ### Platform design and participation quality
 
 When ODI socialized the idea internally and with local officials, people asked: "Isn't this just more social media? Isn't this just going to be another toxic stew? We already have Nextdoor, Reddit—why do we need this?" Marino's response was that the platform—built on Othello—was "intentionally designed by humans motivated to drive meaningful public engagement and deliberation."
 
 Several design choices mattered. The engagement was time-boxed: people were invited for a specific conversation, not an open-ended forum. Participants agreed to a Pledge of Civility upon joining—"It's simple: users promise to be constructive. It's remarkable how effective this is." Human moderators reviewed content, though fewer than 5% of comments were removed, mostly commercial advertisements. Participants could see results updated in real time—how they voted, how the community voted, and distributions across topics. This made engagement feel participatory rather than, as Marino put it, "comments disappearing into a void."
 
 The platform indexed toward consensus rather than majority rule—defined as high support combined with low opposition. Policy options in the second phase were structured around real tensions: fast-tracking permitting versus undergrounding power lines, speed versus careful rebuilding, density versus neighborhood character. Framing choices as trade-offs generated richer dialogue than abstract policy questions.
 
 ### 
 
 ### AI as infrastructure for listening
 
 Weinberg framed AI's value in terms of capacity: "We've all been to stakeholder meetings or public engagements where people submit comments online, and before AI, we really weren't able to do much with it. Humans are not good at dealing with mountains of qualitative data." The technology enabled what he called "listening at scale.”
 
 The team used Claude Sonnet integrated through Snowflake, which simplified procurement since the AI was already available natively in the state's data infrastructure. ODI's data engineers built a pipeline to extract information from Othello into Snowflake, then ran topic modeling and used the LLM to pull key themes and connect them to verbatim quotes. The combination of abstract themes with real voices proved powerful for reporting to the governor's office.
 
 Importantly, the team emphasized keeping humans in the loop: "We double-check everything, we make our own sense of the sense the tools create." And they made a deliberate choice to focus on extracting "know-how"—what people want to happen—rather than just sentiment. "We started with 'How do people feel?'" Marino explained, "but quickly realized our goal was: What do people want to happen?" For program goals, actionable insights mattered more than emotional mapping, though sentiment analysis remained valuable for showing residents they had been heard.
 
 AI was positioned as backend infrastructure, not a front-facing feature. When asked about negative attitudes toward AI among participants, Marino said there was "not nearly as much as expected." Weinberg added: "We didn't lead with AI—it was backend infrastructure. AI is just another tool; if used well, it's helpful."
 
 The biggest risk Marino identified was capture—either by executive leadership or by special interests. The program remains fragile, requiring balance between proximity to power (necessary to drive action) and independence. "Leadership will change in 14 months," Marino noted, referring to the gubernatorial transition. "We need strategies to preserve the integrity of the program."
 
 Scaling presents its own challenges. Other state departments lack ODI's data science capacity. Marino suggested that ODI could evolve into a center of excellence—providing the technical backbone while agencies manage community outreach, audience recruitment, and on-the-ground engagement. This modular approach would let departments run deliberative processes without building their own data teams.
 
 Weinberg emphasized that representation is an ongoing concern. Future iterations will incorporate sortition—random, representative selection of participants—to avoid the biases inherent in self-selected engagement. The team is planning a civic assembly in Oakland using this methodology. They also see potential in applying these tools to regulatory comment processes, where everyday residents are typically drowned out by organized interests.
 
 **Why now**
 
 Beth raised Carolyn Lukensmeyer's point that deliberative engagement has a long history — decades before Audrey Tang's work in Taiwan. So what's different now? Weinberg pointed to the qualitative data problem: "I've been part of huge in-person deliberative polling exercises. In those, you get amazing depth—but it's hard to understand what is actually happening in aggregate." AI enables focus: What did quieter voices say? What did this demographic emphasize? "With large qualitative datasets and thoughtful humans guiding the process, AI can actually help us listen better than we could in a room where a few voices dominate."
 
 Marino added a practical dimension: political environments demand speed. Doing this asynchronously and using AI to convert large amounts of information into actionable insights—without requiring massive facilitation resources—helped the team deliver something meaningful under pressure.
 
 ### 
 
 ### Implications for practice
 
 Several threads from the discussion carry implications for practitioners elsewhere. First, executive commitment matters—not just symbolic support, but willingness to act on what emerges. Weinberg emphasized that without decision-makers at the table, you risk "engaging residents and then producing nothing of substance—which is worse than doing nothing."
 
 Second, framing matters for buy-in. Chris Bui asked about convincing municipalities to partner. Weinberg's advice: explain how this solves problems government workers are actually tasked with solving. "'Democracy isn't good enough' is not a problem agencies are tasked to solve. They are tasked with getting better information for service delivery, regulatory design." Stephen Buckley reinforced this—simple stories based on real applications ("where to put a bike lane") work better than abstract democracy-saving rhetoric.
 
 Third, legal frameworks constrain innovation. Public comment laws often prevent new engagement methods. Working with agencies early to legalize new processes is essential.
 
 Finally, both speakers agreed on the most important advice: "Start. It's always the hardest part. We began by putting one foot in front of the other and just didn't stop."
 
 ### 
 
 ### For Course Adaptation
 
 This session offers several teaching threads. The Engaged California case demonstrates what it takes to move from pilot to policy: executive commitment, intergovernmental coordination, internal technical capacity, and careful attention to legitimacy and representation. The tension between speed and depth—between political timelines and methodological rigor—runs throughout. The choice to focus on "know-how" over sentiment reflects a broader question about what public input is actually for. And the candid discussion of risks (capture, sustainability, leadership transitions) provides realistic grounding for students who might otherwise see only the success story.
 
 ### 
 
 ### Audience Notes
 
 **Questions from chat:**
 
 **Richard:** Is this Claude out-of-the-box? How sophisticated was the topic modeling? Can others replicate this—was it good prompting by humans, or more technical?
 
 **Chris Bui (Better Together America):** How did your experience at California Forward inform this? Do you think the regional sustainability network is a good platform for this kind of engagement?
 
 **Chris Bui:** How do we get accurate representation? In Emeryville, we used a consistent group of 200 residents.
 
 **Siseko Siwali (South Africa):** How are you dealing with true data versus accurate data? True data is lived experience; accurate data is measured or topic-based. They sometimes conflict.
 
 **Stephen Buckley:** Was there anything more systematic than anecdotal feedback on user experience—like a survey—so others who replicate this can compare apples to apples?
 
 **(General chat):** Concerns about astroturfing, bots, and organized lobbying campaigns skewing results at scale.
 
 ### Selected Quotes
 
 **Micah Weinberg:** "These tools allow us to listen at scale. And if you are truly listening, you hear a lot of different things."
 
 **Jeffery Marino:** "One of the greatest innovations here was simply that we were able to get started on something like this, and we had the full support of the administration."
 
 **Participant (follow-up survey):** "I've been reaching out to everyone involved in the recovery effort and received not one reply. Not slammed doors—just no one answering my knock."
 
 **Micah Weinberg:** "Big tech vendors rarely understand state processes. Without that expertise, you risk engaging residents and then producing nothing of substance—which is worse than doing nothing."
